description: We are Seraj Team, 5 passionate creators bridging the gap between complex space science and kids. We believe the future of STEM education lies in gamification. By combining our expertise in Web Development, Game Engineering and UI/UX Design, we built Astroberry. Our mission is to turn real NASA data into an unforgettable, interactive Mars survival adventure for the next generation!
summary:
Astroberry is an interactive, browser-based educational game for children aged 7–12. Players act as mission commanders of a human outpost on Mars, managing oxygen, water, food, and power for a crew of astronauts.

The problem: Most learning materials present space facts, while most space games focus on entertainment without reflecting real engineering constraints. Children rarely experience the decisions that determine whether a mission succeeds or fails.

Our solution: Across six progressive missions, players face real engineering trade-offs: reducing heating saves electricity but affects the crew. After every decision, the game explains what happened, why it happened, and which scientific concept it represents. Failure becomes a lesson: the game explains the cause and lets children try a new strategy.

Real NASA data: DONKI space-weather events drive solar-threat scenarios, Perseverance MEDA measurements shape temperature and dust conditions, and OSDR research informs health-related explanations. Real data and simulated gameplay values are clearly separated and labeled as live or archived.

Why this challenge: It combines NASA science, open data, and STEM education to inspire young learners. The game is built with React and JavaScript and hosted on Vercel, allowing children to play instantly in any browser with no installation required.
details:
Astroberry is an interactive, browser-based educational game where children aged 7–12 become commanders of a Mars outpost. Players manage oxygen, water, food, and power across six progressive missions. Each decision creates a trade-off: for example, reducing heating saves power but can affect the crew. The game simulates these consequences through a daily turn-based system, then provides immediate feedback explaining what happened and the scientific concept behind it.

The main benefit is learning by doing. Instead of only reading about space, children make decisions, experience their consequences, learn from failure, and try new strategies. This develops scientific understanding, critical thinking, resource management, and problem-solving while keeping the experience engaging. Parents and teachers also get an accessible, no-installation STEM learning tool.

Our intended impact is to help young learners understand that space exploration is not only about discovering planets, but also about solving complex engineering problems and keeping people alive in extreme environments.

The project was developed using React.js, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Framer.js, GitHub, and Vercel, with OpenCode and Manus used as AI-powered development and research assistants. NASA open data from DONKI, MEDA, and OSDR was integrated to make scenarios scientifically grounded.

Astroberry is creative because it combines real NASA data, simplified engineering trade-offs, and game-based learning in a child-friendly experience. We considered the target age, accessibility, scientific accuracy, gameplay balance, clarity of feedback, resource limitations, and the need to clearly distinguish real NASA data from simulated gameplay values.
